title: The Destructor That Did Not Run: Inheritance, Virtual Dispatch and the Two Lines Every Interface Needs

questions.question: A Thermometer owning one heap string is created with new, held as a Sensor*, and deleted. The base destructor is not virtual. What happens?
options: Both destructors run, because delete knows the real type from the allocation
The compiler refuses to compile the delete
Only the Sensor destructor runs, the string and its buffer are abandoned, and the whole thing is undefined behaviour
The program crashes immediately, which is how you find the bug
questions.explanation: Measured in the lesson with replaced global operator new and delete: 2 allocations still live with a non-virtual base destructor, 0 with a virtual one. Two, because the string object and its buffer are both lost.

questions.question: The same object read 21.5 through a const LooseSensor& and 0 through a LooseSensor taken by value. Why did the second one not fail or warn?
options: The by-value parameter was const, which disabled the override
The copy really is a LooseSensor
Virtual dispatch does not work on copies
The compiler optimised the call away and returned a default
questions.explanation: Virtual dispatch correctly picked the base implementation; the derived part was never copied. sizeof(LooseSensor) is 8 and sizeof(LooseThermometer) is 16. The copy is eight bytes and the rest has nowhere to go. That is slicing: legal, silent on gcc and clang, and silent even under clang's -Weverything.

questions.question: Why does this lesson's test suite assert std::has_virtual_destructor<Sensor> instead of demonstrating the leak?
options: Because the leak is too small to measure reliably
Because has_virtual_destructor is faster than running the destructor
Because the leak only happens on Windows
Performing the delete is undefined behaviour, so the address sanitizer stops the program rather than yielding a measurement
questions.explanation: This is the one trap in the lesson that cannot be tested at runtime. The answer is not to test for it but to require it, with one static_assert per interface next to the declaration.

questions.question: A base declares double read() const and a derived defines double read() without const, with no override keyword. What have you got?
options: A correct override, because const is not part of the signature
A correct override, but one that cannot be called through a base pointer
A new, non-virtual function that hides the base one, so the answer depends on whether the caller holds a base or a derived reference
A compile error, because the signatures do not match
questions.explanation: Overriding needs the name, parameter types, constness and reference qualification to agree exactly. Dropping const is the most common near miss because it reads correctly in both places. Writing override turns it into an error at the declaration.

questions.question: gcc warns about deleting through a non-virtual base destructor in one case and not another. Which case is silent on both gcc and clang?
options: A base with no virtual functions at all, such as a handle or a resource wrapper
Neither; both compilers always warn
An abstract base with pure virtual functions
A base with at least one other virtual function
questions.explanation: Nothing marks such a class as polymorphic, so the compiler has no reason to suspect it is a base. That is exactly the shape this bug tends to take, which is why the static_assert is worth more than the warning.

questions.question: Why does no value type in librc, including rc::math::Pose, have a virtual destructor?
options: Value types cannot have virtual functions in C++17
One virtual function costs one hidden pointer per object
Because adding one would make them non-copyable
Because the sanitizer reports virtual destructors on value types
questions.explanation: A million readings would pay eight megabytes for dispatch they never use. Measured in the lesson: sizeof went from 16 to 24 on a 64 bit platform when one virtual function was added, and the cost is per object rather than per class. An interface is for things you swap; a value is not one.
